questions.question: What does it mean for a square matrix $A$ to be diagonalizable?
options: Every entry outside the main diagonal of $A$ is already zero.
There is an invertible $P$ such that $P^{-1}AP$ is diagonal.
There is a diagonal $P$ such that $AP=0$.
There is a matrix $P$ such that $PAP$ is the identity.

questions.question: What is the role of the columns of $P$ in a diagonalization?
options: They are arbitrary nonzero vectors.
They are the rows of $A$.
They are the diagonal entries of $D$.
They are independent eigenvectors of $A$.

questions.question: Why is an already diagonal matrix diagonalizable?
options: Take $P=I$, so $P^{-1}AP=A$ is diagonal.
Every diagonal matrix has determinant $0$.
A diagonal matrix has no eigenvectors.
Diagonalizability is defined only for non-diagonal matrices.

questions.question: What does diagonalizability say about a linear operator after changing basis?
options: Its action becomes coordinate-wise scaling.
Its action becomes nonlinear.
It loses all eigenvalues.
It sends every vector to zero in the new basis.

questions.question: A $3\times3$ matrix has eigenvalues $1$, $2$, and $3$. What can be concluded?
options: It has only one eigenvector.
It must be the identity matrix.
It is defective.
It is diagonalizable.

questions.question: Does a repeated eigenvalue automatically prevent diagonalizability?
options: No. Repeated eigenvalues automatically create extra eigenvectors.
No. It is allowed if it has enough independent eigenvectors.
Yes. Every repeated eigenvalue makes the matrix defective.
Yes, unless the matrix also has a nonzero determinant.

questions.question: Why must $P$ be invertible in $P^{-1}AP=D$?
options: Because diagonal matrices cannot multiply noninvertible matrices.
Its columns must form a basis, so the change of basis is reversible.
Because $A$ must be singular.
Because every matrix product requires invertible factors.

questions.question: A $3\times3$ matrix has $am(2)=2$, $gm(2)=2$, $am(5)=1$, and $gm(5)=1$. Is it diagonalizable?
options: No, because the eigenvalue $2$ is repeated, so there are too few eigenvectors.
Yes, because the algebraic multiplicities $2+1$ add up to $3$.
Yes, the multiplicities match for every eigenvalue.
No, because $am(2)=2$ means the eigenvalue $2$ needs a Jordan block.

questions.question: A $2\times2$ matrix has characteristic polynomial $(λ-3)^2$ and eigenspace for $3$ equal to $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}$. Is it diagonalizable?
options: Yes, because the algebraic multiplicity is $2$.
No, because every repeated eigenvalue makes the determinant zero.
Yes, because the eigenvalue is real.
No, it has only one independent eigenvector.

questions.question: The quarter-turn rotation $\boldsymbol{R}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2+1$. Which statement is correct?
options: It is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$, but it is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{C}$.
It is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$, since its eigenvalues $\pm\mathrm{i}$ are distinct.
It is defective, so it is diagonalizable over neither $\mathbb{R}$ nor $\mathbb{C}$.
It is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$, since it is invertible with determinant $1$.

questions.question: For square real matrices, which statement about diagonalizability and invertibility is true?
options: Every invertible matrix is diagonalizable.
Every diagonalizable matrix is invertible.
A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it is invertible.
Neither property implies the other.
